data.caption: velverdo.com
data.copy:
I had a dental emergency on a Mediterranean cruise. The ship's dentist was from Germany. He asked me ONE question that made my American dentist look 15 years behind.

I'm 58 years old.

My husband and I saved for two years for this cruise. Two weeks through the Mediterranean. Greece, Italy, Spain.

Day three, we're at dinner.

I bite into a breadstick.

Sharp pain shoots through my front tooth.

Not just sensitivity. Real pain.

I drop the breadstick. Put my hand to my mouth.

My husband looks worried. "You okay?"

I try to drink water. The cold hits my tooth and I wince.

I can't eat. Can't drink. The pain is constant now.

That night, I can barely sleep.

The next morning, I go to the ship's concierge.

"I need to see a dentist."

She makes a call. Gets me an appointment that afternoon with the ship's dentist.

His office is small. Clean. On Deck 3 near the medical center.

Dr. Weber. German accent. Maybe mid-50s.

He examines my tooth. Takes an X-ray with a portable machine.

"You have some inflammation," he says. "The root is exposed here because of recession. That's causing the sensitivity."

He applies something to the tooth. The pain eases immediately.

"This will help for now," he says.

Then he looks at my gums more closely.

"How long has your recession been this severe?" he asks.

"About three years," I say. "My dentist back home has been monitoring it."

"Has he discussed collagen therapy for your recession?"

I stare at him.

"What's that?"

He looks at me for a moment. Then sets down his tools.

"Your gums are made almost entirely of collagen," he says. "It's the structural protein that holds the tissue together and keeps it attached to your teeth."

"After age 30, your body produces less collagen every year. By 50, you're making about half as much as you did at 25."

"So your gums—no matter how clean they are—start breaking down because they're running out of the material they're made of."

"At my sister's funeral, I looked down at my belly.
She died at 61 from complications of diabetes. I'm 54. Same body type. Same blood sugar climbing. I had seven years."

I'm an endocrinology nurse. I've worked in diabetes management for 20 years.

My sister, Karen, died three weeks ago. Diabetic ketoacidosis. Kidney failure. Cardiac arrest. She was 61.

At her funeral, I stood at the casket. Looked at her face. Then looked down at my own belly.

Karen gained 37 pounds during menopause. All midsection. Her waist went from 28 inches to 39 inches between ages 50 and 58.

At 58, type 2 diabetes diagnosed. At 60, first hospitalization for blood sugar crisis. At 61, dead.

I'm 54. My belly looks exactly like hers did at 54. My fasting glucose is climbing. My waist is 38 inches.

Seven years until 61. Seven years to avoid her fate.

The Body I Recognized :

Here's what they don't tell you about being a diabetes nurse watching your sister die:

You know exactly what killed her. You've counseled hundreds of patients through the same progression. Central obesity. Insulin resistance. Type 2 diabetes. Complications. Death.

And you're watching it happen to your own body.

From 49 to 54, I gained 37 pounds. Every pound central. My waist from 29 inches to 38 inches.

I'd see Karen at family dinners. Notice her belly growing. Notice mine growing the same way.

I knew we were following the same path. I just didn't know how to stop it.

The Numbers That Sentenced Me :

My labs three months after Karen's funeral:

Waist: 38 inches (Karen's was 38 at 54)
Weight: 179 pounds (Karen was 176 at 54)
Fasting glucose: 122 (prediabetic, Karen's was 119 at 54)
A1C: 6.4% (prediabetic, Karen's was 6.3% at 54)
Triglycerides: 251 (very high, Karen's were 248 at 54)
Blood pressure: 148/92 (Karen's was 146/90 at 54)

The numbers were nearly identical. Same timeline. Same metabolic profile. Same central obesity pattern.

data.copy:
I gave my cat taurine every single day for two years to protect her kidneys. Last month her vet told me she's in stage 3 kidney failure. 

More than half her kidney function is already gone.

Years of taurine every morning. Mixed into her food. And her kidneys were quietly failing the entire time I thought I was protecting them.

My name is Debra. I live in Columbus with my husband and our cat Nala. 

She's an 11 year old tabby who has slept on my pillow every single night since I adopted her at 2. 

She follows me into the bathroom. She sits on my laptop when I'm working. 

She is the most annoying, needy, perfect cat I've ever had and I would do anything for her.

About two years ago I started seeing stuff online about kidney problems being the number one killer of cats. 

The stat that got me was "1 in 3 cats will develop it." I looked at Nala and thought ok, not you. I'm going to get ahead of this.

I did what most of you have probably done.

I bought a stainless steel water fountain. Watched her drink from it. Felt good.

Switched her to expensive kibble and wet food. High quality.

And then I found taurine. Saw the research about how cats can't make it on their own. How it's critical for kidney function. Heart function. Everything.

I ordered it. Started giving her 500mg every single morning mixed right into her wet food. She ate it no problem.

And I genuinely believed I had handled it.

Fountain. Wet food. Taurine. Annual vet visits. 

I was doing more than anyone I knew. I felt like one of the responsible ones.

For two years I had this quiet confidence that Nala was covered.

Then last month I took her in for her regular checkup. Nothing was wrong. She was eating fine. Playing. Purring. Being Nala. 

I almost didn't do the bloodwork because everything seemed normal and it's not cheap. 

But I figured why not, she's 11, let's just check.

Three days later my vet called.
Stage 3 CKD.

I said the thing you would have said.

I left my dog with my neighbor for a week. 

When I came back, I didn't recognize her.

Not because she looked different.

Because she acted like a completely different dog.

No scratching. Shiny coat. Running around like a puppy.

For two weeks, I tried to figure out what my neighbor did while I was gone.

What I finally discovered made my jaw drop.

And made me realize my vet has been hiding something from me for years.

My name is Debbie Ann. I'm 46. I live in Minneapolis, Minnesota.

And I need to tell you what happened because I think your vet is hiding the same thing from you.

Let me start from the beginning.

Two years ago, I adopted a dog named Lily from the shelter.

She was perfect. Beautiful. Sweet.

But she scratched constantly.

Every single day. All day long.

Sometimes she had hot spots. Sometimes she didn't.

Sometimes she'd chew her paws till she bled.

I took her to the vet.

"It's environmental allergies," she said. "Very common."

She prescribed Apoquel. $180 a month.

Lily still scratched.

I went back.

"Could be a million different things," she said. "Let's try a hydrolyzed diet and a medicated shampoo."

$220 for the food. $45 for the shampoo.

Lily still scratched.

I tried everything.

Coconut oil. Fish oil capsules. Oatmeal baths. Benadryl. A Cytopoint injection. Collagen chews from Amazon.

Nothing worked.

For two years, I just accepted it.

"Dogs just scratch. It's what they do."

That's what my vet kept saying.

Then last summer, my husband surprised me with a month-long trip to Europe.

Paris. London. Rome. Barcelona.

I was so excited.

But then I realized: what do I do with Lily?

My friends were all busy.

Boarding was too expensive for a whole month.

Then I remembered my neighbor, Becky.

She lives two doors down. Mid-60s. Retired. Really sweet.

We'd talked a few times. She mentioned she loved dogs.

I knocked on her door one afternoon.

Dr. Hollis's retirement letter came on a Tuesday.

I sat at the kitchen table staring at it. Dr. Hollis had seen Josie since she was eight weeks old. He knew her whole story. The hot spots that showed up her first spring. The ear infection that August. The paw licking that started the winter she turned two.

And he knew about Duke, the shepherd I had before her, because Duke was his patient too. He knew exactly why I flinched every time a prescription pad came out. He always said the same thing. "She's three, Paul. Let's keep working the food and the gut angle before we sign her up for a lifetime prescription."

Prepared. Modern. Informed.

data.caption: everflite.co
data.copy:
My son hasn't let me comfort him since he was nine years old.

I know the exact moment it stopped.

Little League. A bad call at second base. He got tagged out - he was safe, everyone in those bleachers saw it - and he walked back to the dugout with that red, crumpling face that kids get right before they fall apart completely. I was on my feet. Arms already open. That mother's instinct, ready to catch him.

And a dad two rows down yelled, "Shake it off, buddy! Be tough!" He shook it off. He was tough. And I haven't been able to catch him since.

He's 27 now. He lives alone in an apartment in Denver. Works in logistics. Has a dog named Biscuit and a secondhand couch and a refrigerator I've personally inspected on FaceTime - 60% condiments, 40% mystery takeout containers.

He's fine. He's always "fine."

That word. Fine. The single most dishonest word in the English language, and my son has built a fortress out of it. For three years, I watched him be "fine" through a brutal breakup. A layoff that stretched eight months. The death of his grandfather - my dad - the man my son quietly measured his entire life against.

Fine. Fine. Fine.

I called every Sunday. I asked the same questions. How's work. How's Biscuit. You eating real food? He answered in three-word sentences. Good. Pretty good. Yeah, Mom. My husband would look at me after I hung up: "How is he, really?" And I had nothing. Because I had watched the world turn my little boy into someone very, very skilled at not telling me.

I am not a woman who gives up.

When my kids were small and sick, I was the one researching symptoms at midnight. When my daughter was struggling in high school, I was the one who found her the right therapist, the right book, the right words at the right time. I am a fixer. It is my spiritual gift and my greatest flaw.

data.caption: metabolae.com
data.copy:
I am in a hospital bed. If you are a type 2 diabetic and your doctor keeps telling you to just take m*tformin and manage your A1c, I am begging you to listen to me right now.

I had a heart attack two weeks ago.

I almost did not make it, and I am writing this because if I had seen something like it a year ago, I would not be here.

I placed my 1,412th coronary stent on October 3rd, 2024.

Sixteen days later, at 2:47 AM on October 19th, I was on the receiving end of one.

I was 58 years old.

I am a board-certified interventional cardiologist. Twenty-two years of practice. Two stents placed in my own left anterior descending artery by a fellow I had trained three years earlier.

I coded on the table for eleven seconds.

The hospital bill was $71,000. Cardiac rehab was another $9,200.

They will let me operate again. My hospital privileges are intact. But I will never place a stent again without remembering that I was on that same table with someone I had trained running a wire into my own artery because everything I was taught to prescribe had not saved me.

I am writing this because I know exactly what my colleagues will say when they see it. I do not care.

If you are over 50 and you have Type 2 diabetes, or someone you love does, please read the entire thing.

I know it is long. I know you are scrolling. I know you have things to do.

Fifteen months ago I would have given anything for someone with my credential to sit me down and tell me what I am about to tell you.

Nobody did.

I was diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes six years ago at 52. Fasting glucose 141. A1C 6.9.

The diagnosis surprised me and it did not. My father had died of a myocardial infarction at 64. He was a Type 2 diabetic managed on M*tformin and a blood pressure pill for eleven years. My mother's blood pressure had been creeping upward for a decade before she passed. data.caption: healpurea.com
data.copy:
I was diagnosed with LPR after a year of suffering from constant coughing spasms, thick sticky mucus in my nose and throat, clogged ears, post nasal drip, leaky bladder caused from the harsh coughing, and trouble functioning without a Vicks Vapor Lozenge or gum in my mouth. Got scoped and saw nothing. Gastro and ENT prescribed PPI, cutting out practically all food except veggies and meat.

I want to stay with that list for a moment.

Because if you have LPR, you know that the list is never just one symptom. It is always the whole cascade. The coughing that becomes so violent it involves your whole body. The mucus that you can clear and clear and clear and it is back within thirty seconds. The ears that feel full and wrong. The lozenge in the pocket that you reach for automatically, not because it fixes anything, but because having something in your mouth is the only way to stay ahead of it for five more minutes.

And the leaky bladder from coughing. The one you don't tell people about because how do you explain that your throat problem is affecting your ability to get through a normal day without a change of clothes. I am telling you about it because when I wrote that forum post, I was done editing the list for other people's comfort. I had been sick for a year and nothing was getting better and I was tired of managing how the information landed.

That was about twenty months ago.

I am 59. Before any of this started I was someone who ran, who traveled, who taught group fitness on Tuesday mornings. I am telling you that not to make a point about who I used to be but because the distance between that version of my life and the version where I could not get through a conversation without coughing, could not eat anything without consequence, could not leave the house without lozenges in every pocket, was the kind of distance that makes a person start to wonder whether they are going to get back.

My son's name was Mason. He died eight months ago. He was twelve.

I do not own a gun. I have never owned a gun. I am writing this from the same kitchen table where I sat with him three nights before the accident and quizzed him on the four rules. Stop. Don't touch. Run away. Tell a grown-up. He nailed them. He laughed at me a little for making him do it again. He said "Mom, I'm twelve, I know."

He did know. He could recite them in his sleep. He had been through the school assembly. He had been through the safety video at his dad's house in Kentucky. He had nodded through every single time I had brought it up over the previous six years.

I am writing this because last Sunday afternoon I sat down on the floor of his bedroom and I went through his phone for the first time since the funeral.

I have had the phone for eight months. I have charged it once a month so the battery would not die completely. I had not opened it. I told my therapist three months ago that I could not open it. She told me there was no timeline for that and not to push myself.

Last Sunday morning I made coffee and I sat in his room and I unlocked it. I had the passcode written on a sticky note in my dresser drawer. I had asked him for it three years ago when I gave him the phone. I told him there would be no privacy from his mother and he had agreed and given it to me and I had written it down and I had never used it.

I want to write down what I found because I want this to exist somewhere that is not just my head.

The first thing I went into was the photos. Most of what was there was what I expected. Selfies with his brother. Videos of him doing kickflips on his skateboard in the apartment complex parking lot. data.copy:
I sat in the clinic parking lot with a $4,500 quote folded in my shirt pocket.

Two years I had spent on the surgery fence. I'm 56, an engineering manager, and I had googled lower blepharoplasty more times than my fantasy team. The bags were that bad. Steamer trunks.

The consult was fine. The surgeon was nice. The math was not. $4,500 for my lower lids. General anesthesia. Ten to fourteen days of bruises to explain in meetings. And insurance only helps if the skin blocks your field of vision. Mine just made people ask if I got into a fight.

I sat in the truck and could not turn the key. It was not only the money. It was the thought of coming back with someone else's eyes. Surgery is permanent in both directions.

That night I had the deposit page open at 1am, cursor on the button. I closed the laptop instead and gave myself one rule. Before the scalpel, I try the last sane step first.

Not filler. My buddy paid $1,200 for tear trough filler and his puffiness was back inside a week. Not Botox near the eyes, I had heard the droopy lid stories. And not another cream. We all know the creams were a money grab.

The step I found was a dissolving microneedle patch. Here is the honest part. A scalpel removes herniated fat, and some men truly need that. But for a lot of us the daily problem is fluid and deflated, crepey skin. That does not need demolition. data.caption: helloholie.com
data.copy:
The terrible truth I learned from her doctor is that for an elderly person, sitting in a favorite recliner is like sitting on a concrete block.

I didn't understand that until the morning I found my mother gripping both armrests of her chair, tears running down her face, unable to stand up.

Not a fall. Not a stroke. Pain. Deep, invisible pain that had been building for months while I thought she was comfortable.

My name is Jennifer. I'm 54. My mother, Helen, is 78.

She's lived with me for two years since her second fall. Her world is her recliner by the front window. That is where she watches her shows. That is where she naps. That is where she eats most of her meals because getting to the kitchen table takes more out of her than it used to.

She sits in that chair for most of the day.

Eight, sometimes nine hours.

I thought that was fine. She was comfortable. She had a memory foam cushion I'd bought her, a good one, not cheap, and it seemed to be working. She wasn't complaining. I wasn't seeing anything alarming when I helped her change at night.

What I didn't know is that the damage was already happening.

It starts invisibly. That's the thing nobody tells you.

The first sign I noticed was that Mom had started shifting more than usual. Just small adjustments. A lean to one side, then back. A subtle repositioning every few minutes that she probably wasn't even conscious of.

I asked if she was uncomfortable.

"No, honey. Just a little restless."

I accepted that. Restless seemed fine.

Three weeks later I was helping her into her nightgown and I saw the red patch on her tailbone for the first time.

Not a wound. Not yet. But a deep, dark red that didn't fade when I pressed it gently with my finger. The kind that looks like it goes deeper than the surface.

My stomach dropped.

I called her doctor the next morning. What he told me in the next three minutes changed everything I thought I knew about keeping my mother safe.

Switching to a different inhaler is not going to clear your lungs.

Not Spiriva. Not Symbicort. Not Trelegy. Not the Mucinex you're maxing out twice a day. Not the mullein tea everyone in your support group swears by.

Heading straight for an oxygen tank. Because for three years I was treating a thinning problem that was never a thinning problem.

And the worst part? Eight months ago my pulmonologist looked me in the face and started talking about "planning ahead" for supplemental oxygen.

I'm done being polite about this. If you have COPD and you're sitting in your support group asking which inhaler to bring up at your next appointment, you are wasting time your lungs do not have.

data.caption: nolara.shop
data.copy:
My mom's home health nurse looked at the bathroom floor, then looked at me, and said the thing no caregiver is ever prepared to hear: "This bathroom is going to put your mother back in the hospital. And when she goes back in this time, she may not come home."

I thought I was doing everything right.

Mom fell four months ago. Middle of the night. Getting up to use the bathroom.

Broke her wrist catching herself on the edge of the vanity.

Emergency room at 4 AM. Surgery the next morning. Six weeks in a cast.

The ER doctor didn't soften it. Falls in elderly women are not accidents. They are warnings.

"Seventy percent of seniors who fall once will fall again within the year," she told me. "And the second fall is almost always worse. Broken hip. Head trauma. That's when families start having the conversation about whether their parent can ever live alone again."

That sentence rearranged my entire life.

Seventy percent fall again within a year.

One in three who fracture a hip never return to independent living. Twenty percent don't survive the first year.

So I did everything they told me to do.

Moved in with her for two weeks after the surgery. Cleared the throw rugs from the hallway. Installed grab bars in the shower, next to the toilet, by the sink. Bought a shower chair. Non-slip mats everywhere. Raised toilet seat.

Spent almost three thousand dollars between the contractor and the equipment.

Mom hated all of it.

"My bathroom looks like a hospital room."

She refused to use the shower chair for the first week because it made her feel like we'd already written her off. She won't use "old people" devices. It's a battle every single time I try to help.

"I'm not dying," she said. "I broke my wrist. Stop treating me like I'm in a nursing home."

But she used it. Because she was scared too. Even if she wouldn't say it.

And then I started cleaning her bathroom.

Because here's the thing nobody tells you about caring for an elderly parent.

Apoquel is not going to fix your dog.

Not Apoquel. Not Cytopoint. Not prescription food. Not the $42 probiotic chews everyone in your Facebook group swears by.

keyword.description: Free-text search string (lowercased server-side). Use for product names, brands, hooks, domains — not for category/niche (use niches).
keyword.allowed_values: Any string; empty = no text filter.

searchkeyword.description: Which ad field keyword searches. NOT a niche/category selector.
searchkeyword.allowed_values: All, landingurl, pagename, adtext, productname. Default All when keyword is set.

countries.description: Ad target countries (where the ad runs — wlads.countries). Not store HQ.
countries.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated ISO2: US, GB, DK, NL, BE, IE, NO, SE, FR, DE, IT, CA, NZ, AU, BR, AT, CH, ES, FI, PL, PT, GR, TR, AE, SA, QA, KW, BH, OM, JO, IL, LB, IQ, EG.
countries.notes: MX/CO/CL are not in this Meta targeting catalog. Use store_based_in for stores based in those markets.

excludeCountries.allowed_values: Comma-separated ISO2: US, GB, DK, NL, BE, IE, NO, SE, FR, DE, IT, CA, NZ, AU, BR, AT, CH, ES, FI, PL, PT, GR, TR, AE, SA, QA, KW, BH, OM, JO, IL, LB, IQ, EG.

storebasedin.description: Store Based In (dashboard storebasedin → store_traffic.shop_origin_country). Use for Mexico/Colombia/Chile/etc. store HQ.
storebasedin.allowed_values: Comma-separated ISO2 including MX, CO, CL, AR, PE and other Explore Shops Based In markets.

niches.description: Product category / vertical filter (dashboard Meta niches). Use when user asks for a category, niche, vertical, or market — not keyword.
niches.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated codes: CG, AM, GG, JY, GS, HT, BY, BG, SK, WC, MC, SP, KS, TS, HE, PS, DP, HI, FT, OG, OP, TR, AC, AA, BM, FK, SH, SW, EL, FW, WT, EW, FR, GM, PH, EC, WE, SC, BE, MU, PA, CB, CF, CP, DC, CT, HH, SG, YG, CC, PZ, LS, GP, WN, SF, OR, MG, PB. See allowed_niches in response for code→label map. Fashion/clothing = CG.

website.description: Detected store/checkout technology on the landing page (dashboard Website filter).
website.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated codes: SH, TP, BU, LS, CC, SL, TA, GG, FU, CS, LP, FO, SI, GP, XS, YC, HY, DI, MS, SB, PP, WC, TT, TW, PI, GO, SC, FB, MG, WP, SQ, PS, GM, KV, CO, HJ, WX, AR, BC, MC. SH=Shopify, WC=WooCommerce, CS=Clickfunnels. See allowed_technologies in response.

languages.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

excludeLanguages.allowed_values: Comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

apps.description: Shopify apps detected on the store.
apps.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated app names/ids from dashboard Apps filter. See allowed_apps in response.

excludeApps.description: Exclude stores using these Shopify apps.
excludeApps.allowed_values: Comma-separated app names/ids. See allowed_apps in response.

themes.description: Shopify theme name on the store (exact match).
themes.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated exact theme names from dashboard Themes filter (discover via GET /api/themes).

scaling.allowed_values: rising, stable, declining, nodownscaling, upscaling, downscaling.

mediafilter.allowed_values: videos, images, carousel, dco. Omit/All = all formats.

pagetypefilter.allowed_values: products, collections, funnels, nofunnels. Empty/All = all types.

adscorefilter.description: WinningHunter ad score tier (Established / Has Potential / Unestablished).
adscorefilter.allowed_values: winning (Established), scaling (Has Potential), testing (Unestablished). Requires matching account tier.

lowimpressions.description: Hide ads with very low impressions.
lowimpressions.allowed_values: hide (exclude low-impression rows). Omit = show all.

rankgrowthfilter.description: Within-brand ad rank momentum vs historic rank_history.
rankgrowthfilter.allowed_values: Comma-separated subset of: rising, stable, declining.

minadrank.description: Minimum within-brand ad rank (lower rank number = stronger ad for that brand, e.g. #1).

min.description: Minimum duplicate/active-seen ad count on the page.

minactiveads.description: Minimum active Meta ads on the advertiser Facebook page (total_active_ads_on_page).
minactiveads.notes: find_winning_products auto-applies minactiveads=50 for US when not set (see forced block).

minactiveadsgrowth.description: Minimum page active-ads percent growth over activeadsgrowthperiod.
minactiveadsgrowth.allowed_values: Human percent (25 = 25%); negatives allowed for decline.

activeadsgrowthperiod.description: Lookback window for active-ads growth filter.
activeadsgrowthperiod.allowed_values: 1w, 1m, 3m. Default 1m when min/max growth set. 1w=1 week, 1m=1 month, 3m=3 months.
activeadsgrowthperiod.notes: 14d/2m exist on the dashboard but are omitted from MCP — sparse wlads baselines return empty result sets.

minpagelikes.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. Ads missing the field excluded when min set.

minadspend.description: Minimum EU ad spend total in adspendtimeframe window.
minadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier; can return upgrade JSON.

maxadspend.description: Maximum EU ad spend in window.
maxadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. 999999 treated as no upper cap server-side.

adspendtimeframe.description: Rolling window ad spend is summed over (NOT a calendar month filter).

minreach.description: Minimum EU reach/views total in reachtimeframe window.
minreach.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

reachtimeframe.description: Rolling window reach is summed over.

mintraffic.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

minproductsonstore.description: Minimum published products on the Shopify store.

minprice.description: Minimum product price on landing page.

mincopylength.description: Minimum ad primary text character length.

minvideolength.description: Minimum video duration in seconds (use with mediafilter=videos).

mindays.description: Minimum days the ad has been running.
mindays.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

from.description: Ad launch date lower bound (Meta started field — when ad began running, NOT scrape date).
from.allowed_values: YYYY-MM-DD. Requires to on same range.

to.notes: To isolate ads running in a calendar month: ad_created_to=last day of month AND fromlastseen=first day of month.

product_from.description: Shopify product creation date lower bound.

pagefrom.description: Facebook page creation date lower bound.

activestatus.description: Legacy dashboard param (no longer applied to ES queries).
activestatus.allowed_values: Ignored — use adstatus or last_seen_from/to instead.

adstatus.description: Dashboard Status filter — recently seen vs stale ads.
adstatus.allowed_values: active (lastSeen or updated_at within last 4 days), inactive (neither field within last 4 days), All/empty (no status filter).
adstatus.notes: find_winning_products forces active. Same as dashboard Status = Active.

sorting.allowed_values: relevance, datefound, mostrecent, lastseen, adspend, longestrunning, reach, adsetamount, consistency, monthlyvisits, monthlytraffic, monthlyrevenue, pageactiveads, toprank, mostsaved. Aliases: rank/top_ad/best_ranked→toprank (asc = best rank first, desc = worst rank first). ad_started→mostrecent. monthly_visits→monthlyvisits. monthly_traffic→monthlytraffic.

page.description: Pagination page index (informational). Deep pagination requires scroll from the previous response — incrementing page alone does not advance the result set.
page.allowed_values: MCP uses 1-based page (1=first page); echoed value is 0-based internal page sent to API.

scroll.description: Opaque pagination cursor. Empty/omit on the first request; pass the response scroll value on the next request with the same filters to fetch more ads. Required to download beyond the first page (especially sort_by=lastseen).
scroll.allowed_values: Opaque string from previous response; empty string or omit for first page. Stop when scroll is null/absent or data is shorter than a full page.

allowed_apps: BOGOS.io Free Gift Buy X Get Y
KB Back In Stock Restock Alert
Sticky Add To Cart Booster Pro
POWR Email Popup Sales Pop Ups
EG Auto Add to Cart Free Gift
SA Request a Quote, Hide Price
Zoorix Sticky Add To Cart Bar
Tada Pop up Spin Wheel Popups
Coupon X: Discount Code Pop Up
SC Back in Stock Restock Alert

mcp_pagination.hint: Pass scroll_next as scroll on the next call with the same filters to continue. Do not rely on page alone.
